newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: FORECAST-Australian wages consistent with low CPI.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Australian wages consistent with low CPI.

text.p: Australian markets are expected to receive paradoxical news on the pace of wages growth on Thursday, but economists said the overall outlook for wages was one consistent with maintaining low inflation.
Wages will show moderation over the three months to February. In fact, the quarterly rise will be the lowest for the past year. But in annual terms wages growth will show a rise.
The median forecast of the 29 economists Reuters surveyed was for a rise of 0.8 percent in average weekly ordinary time earnings (AWOTE), taking the annual growth rate to 4.3 percent.

In the fourth quarter, wages rose 1.2 percent to be 3.9 percent higher over the year. The annual rate increases despite the lower quarterly result because the low 0.4 percent result in the first quarter of 1996 drops out of annual calculations.
Forecasts for the first quarter centre range from 0.5 to 1.1 percent, leading to annual rates between 4.0 and 4.6 percent.
Wages are closely watched by the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA), which has warned that wages pose the major threat to maintaining low inflation.
Wages growth of 4.5 percent is seen as the RBA's "line in the sand", above which they are a threat to low inflation.

Recent news on wages, including last week's "living wage" decision of a rise of A$10 per week for low income earners, has been favourable for the wages outlook, and dampened some of the expectation ahead of Thursday's data.
"Overall, wage developments over the last few months suggest that growth in AWOTE should remain in the 4.0 to 4.5 range through 1997," GIO Australia economist Akis Haralabopoulos said.
A quarterly result under 1.0 percent would be positive for continued low inflation, and consistent with other indicators of only moderate inflation pressures in the economy, analysts said.
As an important indicator of inflation, a low AWOTE figure may increase expectations that there is room for another rate cut in the next six months or so.

But economists feel that the positive wage and inflation outlook has been well factored into the market, and it is now activity numbers that will determine rates. With signs of the economy strengthening through 1997, a cut is seen as unlikely.

"With indicators generally pointing to an economy strengthening as the year progresses, the economy should be on a relatively strong path into 1998, the labour market will be stronger, and wage bargaining power is likely to pick up,"
Hambros fixed income economist Su-Ling Ong said.
"With this type of outlook, we suspect that the (RBA) governor will be happy to keep rates on hold," she said.

While AWOTE is seen by many, including the RBA, as the best measure of wages growth in the economy, cutbacks in the public sector appear to have affected lower paid workers most, creating an artificial increase in total AWOTE.
In the fourth quarter last year, annual private sector wages growth stood at 2.8 percent, while public sector wages rose by 7.6 percent. The next data on this break up is due on May 22.
Private sector wages growth is seen as a better indicator of inflation pressures, as the private sector wages are seen as more reflective of the costs to business.
